title: Define readable projections and lossless content formats
description:
## Question

How should Jira issue fields/comments and Confluence page bodies/comments be projected for agent-readable output while preserving exact authoritative content for Version Tags and lossless modification? Decide Aggregate versus Field Resources, Markdown or structural rendering, native ADF/storage-format access, metadata headers, unsupported constructs, and round-trip requirements.

notes.content:
Resolution

### Authority and representation

Readable and authoritative surfaces are deliberately separate. Jira issue, Confluence page, and comment Aggregates are read-only Markdown projections. Independently addressable Field Resources are the only mutation surface and expose exact native content.

Every `jira://<site>/issues/<issue-id>/fields/<field-id>` Resource contains one canonical JSON value. Ordinary values use `application/json; charset=utf-8`; ADF values retain the complete ADF tree and use `application/vnd.atlassian.adf+json; charset=utf-8`. Canonical JSON follows an RFC 8785-style deterministic encoding so object member order and insignificant whitespace cannot churn identity while null, empty strings, arrays, objects, numbers, and unknown ADF members remain distinct and lossless.

Every current or historical Confluence page body and every Confluence comment body uses the exact storage-format UTF-8 string returned for that representation, identified as `application/vnd.atlassian.confluence.storage+xml; charset=utf-8`. ResourceFS does not normalize whitespace, convert it to ADF, or use rendered `view` HTML as authority. Historical version bodies remain read-only.

### Readable Aggregates

A local deterministic renderer maps supported Jira ADF and Confluence storage constructs to `text/markdown; charset=utf-8`; it never calls Atlassian's rendering/conversion endpoints as a fallback. A Jira issue Aggregate renders every visible field in stable field-ID order with display name, native type, current mutability, and canonical Field reference. A Confluence page Aggregate renders the current body. Parent issue/page Aggregates link comment collections but do not inline comments or couple themselves to comment pagination.

Each comment Aggregate renders its body and carries read-only identity, author, timestamps, ownership/container, parent/reply, and visibility metadata. Confluence inline-comment selection, match index/count, resolved state, and dangling state are Aggregate metadata; they are never injected into the authoritative body Field.

An unsupported but well-formed ADF node or storage construct becomes a deterministic typed marker at its source position, with the authoritative Field reference, plus a `Projection warnings` section. It is never silently omitted, invented, or treated as round-trippable Markdown. Malformed native content fails the read instead of returning a partial projection.

### Version Tags and headers

A mutable Field Version Tag hashes exactly the native encoding ResourceFS exposes: canonical JSON bytes for Jira/ADF and exact storage-format UTF-8 bytes for Confluence. Raw HTTP envelope bytes and rendered Markdown are not mutation authority. Commit-time authoritative preflight compares that tag immediately before mutation, and the authoritative response or refetch produces the post-write tag. A Confluence page/comment version number remains separate adapter state and readable metadata; it never substitutes for the public `sha256:<64-lowercase-hex>` Version Tag.

A read-only Aggregate Version Tag hashes the deterministic Markdown bytes actually returned. It names that projection only and is never accepted as a mutation precondition.

The generic plain `rfs_read` envelope gains a `Content Type:` line matching structured output's existing `contentType`. Mutable Field content contains no frontmatter or other in-band ResourceFS metadata, so the bytes copied from a native Field are valid replacement input.

### Mutation and round-trip contract

Existing Atlassian Field replacement is full native replacement through `rfs_write(path, content, ifVersion)`. Markdown-to-ADF/storage replacement is unsupported, and Atlassian Fields do not support hashline `rfs_edit`. Jira Fields report `mutable: true` only when the Site Mount grants update, current edit metadata supports a lossless full `set`, and ResourceFS supports the field's native encoding. Incremental-only and workflow-specific operations remain read-only rather than being synthesized from a replacement.

The round-trip invariant is: a native Field read can be submitted unchanged as `rfs_write` content with its Version Tag without representation loss; parsing and re-encoding Jira JSON yields the same canonical bytes, while Confluence storage bytes are preserved exactly. Unknown native members survive; validation rejects malformed content before egress. Creation Target document formats remain for the downstream creation/mutation decision and are not implicitly committed to Markdown here.

Evidence: **Map Atlassian support onto ResourceFS source architecture** (`rfs-4srt`), **Characterize Jira Cloud issue contracts** (`rfs-4df1`), **Characterize Confluence Cloud page contracts** (`rfs-teei`), and **Define canonical Atlassian site and Path Reference model** (`rfs-lcuh`).
Closed: Native authoritative Fields, deterministic readable Aggregates, content-type headers, unsupported-construct markers, Version Tag bases, and native-only replacement are decided.

title: Define Atlassian browse and search semantics
description:
## Question

How should bounded project/space browsing and Jira/Confluence search map onto ResourceFS tools and Path References? Decide native JQL/CQL exposure versus a common abstraction, result resources, ordering, pagination and Recovery References, query validation, permissions-filtered results, and navigation from results to canonical resources.

notes.content:
Resolution

### Interface and Path References

Atlassian browsing and native query execution remain behind the existing five-tool interface. Fixed network collections are read with `rfs_read`; `rfs_glob` remains unsupported for Atlassian. `rfs_search` keeps its uniform Rust-regex/PCRE2 contract and may search the exact rendered page of an explicit browse or query Resource, but its `pattern` never changes meaning to JQL or CQL.

A new **Atlassian Query Resource** is a read-only collection scoped to one Atlassian Site Mount. Native query languages are exposed without a common abstraction:

```text
jira://<site>/search/<percent-encoded-jql>
confluence://<site>/search/<percent-encoded-cql>
```

The query is one non-empty, canonically percent-encoded UTF-8 segment. Existing Path Reference safety rules and the 64 KiB total reference ceiling apply; the operational decision may lower the effective decoded-query ceiling where live upstream request limits require it. Jira uses enhanced `/rest/api/3/search/jql`; Confluence uses v1 `/wiki/rest/api/content/search` because v2 has no CQL endpoint and the general v1 search result family adds non-content shapes and legacy pagination without improving canonical navigation. Queries never fan out across Site Mounts.

Offset endpoints continue with a validated `:offset:<n>` selector. Token or relative-link endpoints continue with a self-contained base64url `:cursor:<opaque>` selector. The adapter validates tenant authority, endpoint family, and query ownership before following continuation state. It neither exposes a raw upstream URL nor hides a cursor in Path Session state.

### Browse and result collections

Fixed collection grammar remains the canonical grammar already decided: Jira projects, project issues, and site issues; Confluence spaces, space pages, site pages, page ancestors, and direct page children. Query Resources add only the two `/search/<query>` families above.

Browse and query pages are read-only deterministic Markdown collection Aggregates. Each record contains the canonical stable-ID Path Reference plus a fixed compact summary:

- Jira project: display key, name, project type/status;
- Jira issue: display key, summary, status;
- Confluence space: display key, name, type/status;
- Confluence page: title, status, canonical space reference;
- hierarchy rows additionally carry child position where the upstream contract supplies it.

Full bodies and full Aggregates require a read of the canonical Resource. Missing optional metadata stays explicitly absent; it is never replaced by an empty/default value.

Fixed flat browse collections sort by stable ID ascending. Jira decimal IDs compare numerically without narrowing into a machine integer; Confluence opaque IDs compare by canonical bytes. Hierarchy collections sort by child position and then stable ID. Native query results preserve upstream order exactly: caller-authored JQL/CQL `ORDER BY` is honored, queries without it carry no repeatable-order guarantee, and ResourceFS never reorders a partial cursor stream.

### Bounds, pagination, and recovery

One logical Atlassian collection page follows endpoint-safe upstream pages until 1,000 records, ten upstream requests, or an upstream terminal marker, whichever comes first. Endpoint-specific request maxima and response-driven terminal markers remain authoritative; the operational decision locks exact per-endpoint sizes from documentation and live evidence.

The next upstream page becomes the typed source continuation. Existing ResourceFS limits and ADR-0006 apply unchanged. When rendered output fits, the typed upstream continuation is `continuationReference`. When the logical page itself spills, `continuationReference` walks the immutable `artifact://` chain and `sourceContinuationReference` names the next upstream page; the text trailer retains the same route. Empty collections render explicitly. A page failure is atomic and never returns a partial page as complete.

### Validation, permissions, and navigation

ResourceFS validates query encoding and bounds, Site Mount authority, returned stable IDs, parent/container ownership, and collection membership. Atlassian validates native syntax and semantics at execution; there is no ResourceFS JQL/CQL parser or separate validation Resource. Documented query HTTP 400 responses map to `invalid_pattern` and retain bounded structured upstream diagnostics. HTTP 401/403 maps to `permission_denied`; direct 404 remains `not_found`. Classification follows typed status/response structure, never error-message string matching.

Every collection is the configured Site Mount credential's visible graph, not a tenant-completeness claim. Objects omitted by Atlassian permission filtering produce no synthetic per-item diagnostic; an empty visible result is explicit. Scopes never override Jira issue security, comment visibility, or Confluence space/page permissions.

Only stable-ID canonical Path References are navigation targets. Keys, names, titles, breadcrumbs, excerpts, and upstream URLs are display metadata. Unsupported Confluence child/search content types produce bounded `unsupported_projection` diagnostics on the owning collection containing the upstream type and stable ID. They are never silently dropped, used as generic identity, or promoted into Resources outside this destination.

Closed: native site-scoped query Resources, browse/query tool mapping, compact result records, ordering, pagination/recovery, validation, credential-visible permissions, unsupported-type reporting, and canonical navigation are decided.

What authoritative Confluence Cloud contracts must a ResourceFS Source Adapter honor for direct page reads, space/page browsing, CQL search, metadata, body representations, versions, ancestors, children, comments, page creation/update, comment creation/editing, pagination, validators or concurrency signals, authentication, permissions, errors, and rate limits? notes.content: Research started on branch `research/confluence-cloud-contracts` in isolated worktree `/tmp/resourcefs-research-confluence-cloud-contracts`. Planned artifact: `docs/research/confluence-cloud-contracts.md`.

Resolution — branch `research/confluence-cloud-contracts`, commit `5205d1f`, artifact `docs/research/confluence-cloud-contracts.md`.

Use Confluence REST v2 for pages, spaces, hierarchy, versions, and footer/inline comments, with v1 retained for CQL search. Canonical page/space/comment IDs should remain opaque strings because response schemas use strings while generated path schemas say int64. Page bodies are representation-tagged strings; storage, ADF, rendered view, and wiki representations are not interchangeable. V2 collections and CQL use opaque server-provided cursor links. Page updates are full version-numbered replacements requiring current version + 1, but the published contract exposes no ETag/If-Match guarantee and does not document 409. Direct children supersedes the deprecated child-pages endpoint; footer, inline, reply, and dangling-comment states are distinct.

Uncertainty: ID routing, body response shapes, CQL freshness/cursor lifetime, stale-version status, create status/body, comment anchoring, permission concealment, and active rate-limit headers require live probes. The generated ID-type mismatch and documented page-create 200 versus conventional 201 are external contract inconsistencies, not confirmed ResourceFS bugs; no local bug ticket was filed.
Closed: Confluence Cloud page, hierarchy, search, comment, mutation, and operational contracts are documented.

Research artifact amendment — the branch commit was amended from `5205d1f` to `7b6acda`. The artifact now records Atlassian's June 1, 2026 Confluence changelog exception: `GET /wiki/api/v2/pages/{id}/versions` caps results at 50 when `body-format` is supplied and still returns 200 for a larger requested limit; without `body-format`, the documented maximum remains 250. title: Compare native Atlassian REST APIs with ACLI
description:
## Question

Which integration substrate can satisfy the destination while preserving ResourceFS as a standalone Portable Source? Compare official native Jira/Confluence Cloud APIs with ACLI using primary evidence: version and support commitments, stable machine-readable output, Jira and Confluence read/search/create/edit/comment coverage, pagination, exact content fidelity, error and rate-limit visibility, authentication ownership, multiple-site targeting, installation/licensing burden, deterministic testing, and live-smoke feasibility.

notes.content: Research started on branch `research/atlassian-substrate` in isolated worktree `/tmp/resourcefs-research-atlassian-substrate`. Planned artifact: `docs/research/atlassian-api-vs-acli.md`.

Resolution — branch `research/atlassian-substrate`, commit `cf02c0f`, artifact `docs/research/atlassian-api-vs-acli.md`.

Primary-source evidence favors a native HTTP client: Jira REST v3 plus Confluence REST v2, retaining documented v1 CQL search where v2 has no equivalent. Native APIs expose authoritative ADF/storage content, operation scopes, pagination, HTTP status/error bodies, and rate-limit headers, and let ResourceFS own site and credential selection. Official ACLI has useful Jira JSON/search/create/edit/comment commands but no published Confluence namespace, no versioned output schema or continuation/header contract, mutable login/switch state, an external binary lifecycle, and a six-month support window. ACLI is therefore at most an optional Jira operator convenience, not the authoritative adapter boundary.

Uncertainty requiring live probes: exact current ACLI binary/help, CLI profile isolation and header/error preservation, conditional-write behavior, tenant-specific limits, and authoritative native body/version behavior. No implementation bug was found.
Closed: Native API and ACLI trade-offs are documented against the destination criteria.

title: Prove the SQL Server TDS transport boundary
description:
## Question

Does the selected in-process Rust TDS client behave well enough on a real SQL Server surface to support the Database Mount contract? Build a throwaway prototype and review concrete evidence for typed scalar/binary/null reads, parameter binding, schema metadata, bounded row streaming, explicit commit/rollback, optimistic conflict detection, TLS validation, authentication, timeout/cancellation, and transport/error classification. Compare a pinned read-only `sqlcmd` probe only as an oracle; do not build production adapter code.

notes.content: Prototype started. Throwaway branch: `prototype/sql-server-tds-boundary`; isolated worktree: `../resourcefs-prototype-sqlserver-tds`; base includes the completed client-selection research. Planned artifacts: `.rfs-w9fe/tds-prototype/` and `.rfs-w9fe/evidence.md`. The probe will use a disposable SQL Server container and `mssql-client` 0.20.2, with no production ResourceFS integration.

Resolution approved by the requester. Branch: `prototype/sql-server-tds-boundary`. Commit: `4e2a54a` (`prototype(rfs-w9fe): prove SQL Server TDS boundary`). Primary evidence: `.rfs-w9fe/evidence.md`; runnable probe: `.rfs-w9fe/tds-prototype/run.sh`. Verdict: conditional yes—keep `mssql-client` 0.20.2 as the production transport hypothesis. On pinned SQL Server 2022 (`16.0.4230.2`), typed scalar/binary/NULL parameters and rows, PK metadata, bounded streaming with cancellation, explicit rollback/commit, rowversion and no-rowversion stale conflicts, strict TLS rejection, SQL authentication failure, timeout, server-side Attention cancellation, same-connection reuse, typed SQL error 208, and pinned `sqlcmd` 18.4 oracle agreement all passed. The wrapper must explicitly bridge stream cancellation, use the nested timeout configuration, commit/rollback or retire every transaction, and use typed row extraction. Trusted-CA TLS, integrated/Kerberos auth, more SQL Server versions/types, measured MAX/LOB bounds, pool reset, and ambiguous network loss around COMMIT remain implementation/live-smoke gates; they do not falsify the seam proved here.

Closed: Requester approved the conditional prototype verdict: `mssql-client` 0.20.2 is viable enough to carry into the Database Mount specification, with residual platform/type/pool/commit-loss checks retained as implementation and live-smoke gates.

Post-resolution source audit, decision unchanged. In `mssql-client` 0.20.2, configured command deadlines do not wrap `query_named`, incremental stream methods, `simple_query`, or raw begin/commit/rollback paths; those require an external deadline plus `CancelHandle`/connection retirement. Configured `Duration::ZERO` means no deadline, while explicit `query_with_timeout(..., Duration::ZERO)` cancels immediately. Production code must not rely on the documented blanket command-timeout claim. Normal query rows must use typed `Row::get`; advertised raw zero-copy accessors do not retain backing slices on the production conversion path. These constraints belong in “Define Database Mount configuration authority and lifecycle,” “Define transactional database mutation and concurrency semantics,” and implementation live-smoke gates.

title: Report cancellation distinctly from an inactive Path Session
description:
## Parent

rfs-jk0d — Build ResourceFS 1.0 as a standalone path-shaped MCP server

## What to build

`ensure_live` reports a cancelled `OperationGuard` as `ErrorCategory::SourceUnavailable` with the message "Path Session is no longer active" — indistinguishable from a genuinely dead session. Cancellation has its own stable category (`Cancelled`) precisely so a caller can tell "you stopped this" from "the session died underneath you", and collapsing them loses that.

Found during rfs-g2z9 Slice 10 (2026-08-23) while fencing C21 (read-path cancellation), and deliberately left alone as out of that slice's scope.

Not currently reachable through HTTPS: `HttpsSource::read` returns `Cancelled` from the source before `ensure_live` runs, so `rfs_read` of an `https://` reference reports cancellation correctly today. The defect is latent — any source that ignores its guard and succeeds surfaces a cancelled operation to the caller as `source_unavailable`. Every future source family reaches this same path, so the blast radius grows with each one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A cancelled operation reports `ErrorCategory::Cancelled` with a message naming cancellation, distinct from an inactive Path Session's `source_unavailable`.
- [ ] A genuinely inactive Path Session still reports `source_unavailable` with its existing message; the two cases are distinguishable by category AND message.
- [ ] The fence drives a source that ignores its guard and succeeds — the case that makes the defect observable — rather than only a source that already returns `Cancelled` on its own.
- [ ] Per the amended falsifiable-design criteria: the fence is anchored at the level the claim names, and a positive control proves the non-cancelled path completes so the assertion is not satisfied by an unrelated failure.
